notice: These three questions calibrate where you start. They are not a test and they are not an assessment of job readiness.

items.context: You run a subscription app. Weekly active users are up 9% month over month, and the number of users who complete the core action at least once a week is down 4%. Nothing else obviously changed. Someone asks you in a meeting what you think is happening.
items.question: What is your first move?

options.label: Split both numbers by acquisition source, tenure, and platform before saying anything
Say the likely explanation is that a marketing push brought in lower-intent users, and check that
Set up interviews with users who stopped completing the core action
Wait another month, since one month of movement is not enough to act on

items.context: Your team has four weeks. There are three candidates: a fix for a bug affecting 3% of users badly, a small feature 40% of users have asked for, and paying down debt that is slowing the team by roughly 20%. Each takes most of the four weeks. Your manager has no strong opinion and says it is your call.
items.question: How do you decide?

options.label: Estimate the cost of each option not happening for a quarter, then pick the one with the worst cost of delay
Ask whether any of the three has a smaller version that fits in one week, and try to do two of them
Fix the bug, because a broken experience for real users comes before anything else
Put it to the team and go with what most of them want to work on

items.context: After three weeks of research you have concluded that a feature your CEO championed publicly is not worth building — the demand behind it is much narrower than it appeared. You have one slot in tomorrow's leadership meeting.
items.question: How do you open?

options.label: State the recommendation and the single strongest piece of evidence, then take questions
Walk through the research in order so the group reaches the conclusion with you
Lead with what you would build instead, and use the research to explain why
Do not raise it in the meeting; speak to the CEO privately first
